goals: Explain what a model, its parameters and training are
Tell supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning apart
Say why a model can't fit noisy data perfectly
cards: A function with knobs (parameters): input in, prediction out.
The knobs of a model, set by training rather than by hand.
Turning the knobs to make the loss on the examples as small as possible.
Average of (prediction − truth)² over the examples: one number for how wrong a model is.
Supervised learns from examples with answers; unsupervised finds structure with no answers.
Why the error stops above zero
Noise: things the inputs don't capture (traffic, lights) can't be predicted by any model of those inputs.

check.q: Which task is a good fit for machine learning rather than a hand-written rule?
options: Recognizing which photos contain a dog
check.why: Nobody can write the rule for 'dog', but examples with answers are easy to collect.

check.q: In minutes = a × km + b, what are a and b?
check.why: km is the input, minutes the output; a and b are the knobs.

check.q: What does gradient descent do at every step?
options: Tries every possible value of each knob
Moves each knob a little in the direction that lowers the error
check.why: It asks which way is downhill for each knob and takes a small step that way, again and again.

check.q: Grouping subway stations whose days look alike, with no labels, is…
check.why: No answers attached: finding structure is unsupervised.

check.q: What really tells you if a model is good?
options: Its error on the examples it trained on
Its error on examples it has never seen
check.why: A model that only fits its training examples may fail on new ones (overfitting, stage 3).

goals: Read and change every code box on the path
Use lists, loops and functions in Python
Replace loops with NumPy, and show data with pandas and matplotlib
cards: The first item: lists count from 0. xs[-1] is the last.
Runs the indented lines once per item of xs.
Defines a function: a named recipe from inputs to an output.
The mean squared error of whole arrays in one line, no loop.
A table: rows of examples, named columns; df['col'] picks a column, df[cond] filters rows.
Free notebooks in the browser, with GPUs: where real ML code runs.

check.why: Counting from 0: xs[0] = 4, xs[1] = 8, xs[2] = 15.

check.q: What does range(1, 5) count?
check.why: range stops before its second number.

check.q: km = np.array([1, 2, 3]). What is 2 * km + 1?
options: An error: you need a loop
check.why: NumPy does the arithmetic on every element at once.

check.q: How does Python know which lines are inside a loop?
check.why: The indented lines under 'for …:' are the loop body.

check.q: In pandas, df[df['km'] > 2] gives…
options: the rows where km is more than 2
check.why: A condition inside df[…] filters rows.

goals: Read a graph and evaluate a function
Use powers, scientific notation and logarithms
Read an ML formula out loud and turn it into code
cards: The power of e that gives x: ln(eᵗ) = t. It undoes eˣ.
ln a + ln b: logs turn products into sums, so models add log-probabilities.
Add up x₁ to xₙ: a loop, or np.sum.
1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ): squeezes any number into (0, 1), with σ(0) = 0.5.
Gradient descent: move the knobs a step η against the gradient of the loss.

check.q: If f(x) = x² − 2x, what is f(3)?
What is 2⁻³?
Why do models add log-probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities?
options: Multiplying thousands of numbers below 1 underflows to 0
check.why: The product gets too small for a computer; the sum of logs stays an ordinary number.

check.q: What is Σᵢ₌₁⁴ 2i?
One step of θ ← θ − η g with θ = 3, η = 0.1, g = 4 gives…

goals: Treat vectors as arrows and compute lengths and dot products
See a matrix as a move of the whole plane
Compute a network layer as a matrix product plus a bend
cards: a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + …: big when arrows agree, 0 at right angles, negative when opposed.
Where î = (1, 0) and ĵ = (0, 1) land after the move.
How much the move scales areas; 0 means the plane is squashed flat and the move can't be undone.
Doing one move after another; the order matters.
relu(W x + b): a move by a matrix, a shift, then a bend.
Without it, stacked layers collapse into one matrix: still just one straight move.

check.q: How long is the vector (3, 4)?
Two vectors have dot product 0. They are…
options: at right angles (or one is zero)
check.why: a·b = |a||b|cos θ, and cos 90° = 0.

check.q: A matrix's determinant is 0. What happened to the plane?
options: It was squashed onto a line (or a point)
check.why: Zero area left: many points land on the same spot, so the move can't be undone.

check.q: Rotate 90° sends î to (0, 1) and ĵ to (−1, 0). Where does (2, 1) go?
Why does a network need ReLU between its matrices?
options: Without a bend, stacked matrices are just one matrix
To keep numbers positive for the computer
check.why: B(Ax) = (BA)x: any stack of matrices alone is a single straight move.

goals: Tell when a system has one, no or infinitely many answers
Find a matrix's rank and know what a low rank means for a dataset
Solve least squares with the normal equations
cards: det = 0: no inverse; Ax = b has no answer or infinitely many.
The number of independent rows (= independent columns): how many equations really count.
Clear each column below its pivot, then solve bottom up; about n³/3 work.
Swap the diagonal, negate the other two, divide by the determinant.
A tiny determinant: the inverse is huge, so small errors in b become big errors in x.
XᵀX w = Xᵀy: the square system whose solution is the least-squares fit.

check.q: Two equations whose lines are parallel and different have…
check.why: Parallel lines never meet: the equations contradict each other.

check.q: A dataset has columns 'area in m²' and 'area in ft²'. What does that do?
options: Lowers the matrix's rank: the weights stop having one best value
check.why: One column is a multiple of the other, so weight can be traded between them forever.

check.q: What is the rank of [[1, 2], [2, 4]]?
check.why: The second row is twice the first: one independent row.

check.q: In code, how should you solve Ax = b?
check.why: Elimination is faster and loses less to rounding than computing the inverse.

check.q: det A = 2 and det B = 3. det(AB) is…
check.why: Areas multiply: 2 × 3.

goals: Estimate a derivative by nudging
Explain the gradient as the steepest-uphill arrow
Run gradient descent and pick a sensible learning rate
cards: How much the output changes per tiny change of the input: the slope.
(f(x+h) − f(x−h)) / 2h: a numerical slope accurate to h².
The arrow of all partial slopes; it points steepest uphill.
Steps overshoot the valley's bottom and bounce or blow up.
Every step is tiny: training crawls.

check.q: f(x) = x². What's the slope at x = 3?
check.why: The derivative of x² is 2x.

check.q: Why does a nudge of h = 1e-15 give a bad slope estimate?
options: The formula is wrong for small h
Rounding: f(x + h) and f(x) agree in almost every digit
check.why: Computers keep about 16 digits, so the difference is mostly rounding noise.

check.q: Gradient descent on x² with learning rate 1.0 from x = 5…
check.why: x − 1.0 × 2x = −x: it bounces forever.

check.q: The gradient of a loss points…
check.why: So training moves the opposite way: minus the gradient.

check.q: Training a line, ∂L/∂w is positive. The update makes w…
check.why: w ← w − η × (positive) goes down, because a bigger w would raise the loss.

goals: Differentiate with the rules (power, product, chain…)
Know the slopes of sigmoid, tanh and ReLU and why gradients vanish
Check a derivative numerically
cards: d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) · g′(x): multiply the slopes along the chain.
Many layers multiply many small slopes, so early layers get almost no signal.
Compare your derivative with a centered difference; relative error under ~1e-7 means it's right.

check.q: What's the derivative of (3x + 1)²?
check.why: Chain rule: 2(3x + 1) × 3.

check.q: What's the derivative of ln x?
check.why: ln undoes eˣ, and its slope is 1/x.

check.q: The biggest slope a sigmoid ever has is…
Why do deep sigmoid networks learn slowly in their first layers?
options: Backprop multiplies slopes of at most 0.25 per layer
check.why: Twenty layers of ≤ 0.25 gives less than 1e-12: the gradient vanishes.

check.q: Your formula and the centered difference differ by a relative error of 0.6. What now?
check.why: Correct derivatives agree to about 1e-7; 0.6 means a real mistake (often a sign).

goals: Take partial derivatives and assemble the gradient
Write the MSE gradient for a linear model as one matrix formula
Read a Jacobian and its shape
cards: The slope along x with every other input held still.
Gradient of MSE for ŷ = Xw
The m × n matrix of every output's slope with respect to every input.
Always the same shape as the thing it differentiates (a weight matrix's gradient is a matrix like it).

check.q: f(x, y) = x²y. What is ∂f/∂x?
check.why: Treat y as a constant: the slope of x²·(const) is 2x·y.

check.q: For ŷ = Xw with n examples, the MSE gradient is…
check.why: Each residual is weighted by its row's features: Xᵀ times the residuals.

check.q: f maps 3 numbers to 2 numbers. Its Jacobian's shape is…
check.why: One row per output, one column per input.

check.q: What is the Jacobian of f(x) = Wx?
check.why: Output i is row i of W dotted with x, so its slopes are row i of W.

check.q: A weight matrix W has shape (4, 3). Its gradient ∂L/∂W has shape…
check.why: One partial derivative per weight: the same shape as W.

goals: Compute probabilities by counting, with the complement and sum rules
Check slippery answers by simulation
Use Bayes' rule, and see why rare conditions give mostly false alarms
cards: P(not A) = 1 − P(A): 'at least one' is easiest as 1 − P(none).
P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B); knowing one changes nothing about the other.
Count inside B only: P(A and B) / P(B).
P(H | E) = P(E | H)·P(H) / P(E): prior × likelihood, normalized.
A good test for a rare condition still gives mostly false positives: the healthy crowd is huge.
Count words per class, add one to every count, add log-probabilities, pick the bigger total.

check.q: What's the chance of at least one six in two dice rolls?
check.why: 1 − (5/6)² = 11/36: no six on both dice is (5/6)·(5/6).

check.q: In Monty Hall, after the host opens a goat door, switching wins…
check.why: Your first pick is right 1/3 of the time; switching collects the other 2/3.

check.q: The first die shows 6. What's P(sum ≥ 10) now?
check.why: Inside 'first die is 6' there are 6 outcomes, 3 of them reach 10+.

check.q: 1% are sick; the test catches 90% and false-alarms on 9%. A positive test means…
options: about a 90% chance of being sick
check.why: 9 true positives vs about 89 false ones per 1000 people: 9/98.

check.q: Why does a spam filter add 1 to every word count?
options: So an unseen word doesn't make a probability exactly 0
check.why: One zero in a product wipes out all other evidence; add-one smoothing prevents it.

goals: Choose between mean and median and spot outliers
Read box plots, histograms and density estimates, and fix skew with logs
Measure how two variables move together, and know when correlation lies
cards: The median is the typical value on skewed data; the mean is what totals need. Outliers drag the mean, not the median.
The typical distance from the mean: √(average squared distance).
(x − mean) / standard deviation: how many standard deviations from the mean.
Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle half; box plots flag points beyond 1.5 IQR.
A long right tail (durations, prices); taking logs often makes it near-normal.
Covariance scaled to [−1, 1]: a straight-line relation only, and a few extreme points can decide it.

check.q: Outage times: mean 8.2 h, median 1.6 h. What's 'typical'?
check.why: 95% of outages are shorter than the mean: a few weeks-long ones inflate it.

check.q: What's the standard deviation of 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 (dividing by n)?
check.why: Mean 5, squared distances sum to 32, /8 = 4, √4 = 2.

check.q: A KDE with a tiny bandwidth turns into spikes. That's like…
check.why: It memorizes the exact points instead of the shape behind them.

check.q: A QQ plot's points curve sharply up at the right end. The data has…
check.why: The biggest values are far bigger than a bell curve would allow.

check.q: Estimated vs actual hours: r = 0.99 over all outages, 0.2 for those under 12 h. Why?
options: A handful of very long outages decide the overall r
Correlation always drops on smaller data
check.why: Covariance multiplies distances from the mean, so a few extreme points dominate.

goals: Find eigenvectors by picture, algebra and power iteration
Explain PageRank as a Markov chain's eigenvector
Run PCA and read how much variance its components keep
cards: A direction a matrix only stretches: Av = λv; λ is the eigenvalue.
det(A − λI) = 0; for 2×2: λ² − trace·λ + det = 0.
Multiply by A and rescale, repeatedly: the vector lines up with the biggest eigenvalue's eigenvector.
The eigenvalue-1 eigenvector of a random surfer's Markov chain, with damping 0.85.
Center the data, take the covariance matrix's top eigenvectors; each eigenvalue is the variance that direction keeps.
λmax / λmin of the Hessian: how stretched the loss valley is, and how slowly gradient descent crawls.

check.q: For [[2, 1], [1, 2]], v = (1, 1) is an eigenvector. Its eigenvalue is…
A rotation by 90° has…
check.why: It turns every arrow, so none stays on its line.

check.q: A 2×2 matrix has trace 2 and determinant −3; one eigenvalue is 3. The other is…
check.why: They add to the trace (3 + (−1) = 2) and multiply to the determinant.

check.q: Why does PageRank need damping (random jumps)?
options: To make it faster to compute
So readers can't get stuck in a corner of pages, and the answer doesn't depend on the start
check.why: With jumps there's one steady state, reached from anywhere.

check.q: PCA's first component is…
options: the direction of largest variance: the covariance matrix's top eigenvector
the first column of the data
check.why: Variance along a unit u is uᵀΣu, largest along Σ's top eigenvector.
